newsitem.title: INDIA: India divestment seen well-timed - fund managers.
newsitem.headline: India divestment seen well-timed - fund managers.

text.p: The Indian government's plan to divest part of its ownership in four state-run firms won approval on Monday from fund managers who described the move as well-timed.
"India is now the hot favourite among emerging markets," said a director of a European investment bank in Bombay.
"Money is pouring in and the market is rising," he said.
The government said on Friday it planned to sell stakes in four firms -- Gas Authority of India Ltd (GAIL), Mahanagar Telephone Nigam Ltd (MTNL), Indian Oil Corp (IOC) and Container Corp of India.

"We are positive on all four," said the head of the Bombay office of a Hong Kong-based brokerage. Most prospective investors did not want to be identified because they are either associated with the divestment programme or hope to do so.
Two of the four companies -- Container Corp and MTNL -- already have a large public shareholding. The others are relatively new and GAIL appears to be a hot favourite with fund managers.
"The GAIL issue will be lapped up by foreign funds in no time," said an official at the broking arm of a Swiss bank in Bombay. He said all four stocks would get a good price.
The four firms are planning a mix of international and domestic offerings, but the details have not been finalised.
Analysts said they expect only IOC to face some problems as the government owes it billions of rupees from an oil subsidy. An oil price hike meant to pay these dues has been deferred.
IOC, with a market capitalisation of $9.0 billion, is the largest among the four firms on the block.
"A lot will depend on the government's schedule," said a fund manager. "They have not appointed lead managers except in the case of IOC," he said.
In the past the government has sat on proposals and lost opportunities, he said.
Investors also welcomed a related development -- the government's plan to provide greater autonomy to select state-run firms in fund raising and expansion programmes.
Currently, state-run firms must seek permission through different layers of bureaucracy for permission to spend above 500 million rupees ($13.9 million) on any project.
"Sometimes it can take as much as 10 years to get the final approval," said an official of refining firm Hindustan Petroleum Corp Ltd, one of the select nine firms.
